disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with onset typically within 3 months of the stressor and clinically significant distress or functional impairment out of proportion to what would be expected. It often presents with anxiety, low mood, or mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct, but does not meet full criteria for another mental disorder and does not represent a normal bereavement reaction. The course is usually self-limited, resolving within 6 months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, though it can become chronic if stressors persist. Clinically, it is distinguished from normative stress reactions by its impact on social, occupational, or academic functioning and from major depressive or anxiety disorders by its subthreshold, stressor-linked symptom profile and time course.

narrative.stressor: About six weeks ago, Lula’s husband was hospitalized unexpectedly after a minor stroke, and she suddenly became his primary caregiver while he recovered at home. Accustomed to planning church events and mentoring youth on a predictable schedule, she found herself juggling medication schedules, follow-up appointments in Macon, and physical therapy visits, all while trying to keep up with choir rehearsals and her commitments at the senior center. Over the following month, her carefully structured routines around gardening, quilting, and church work began to unravel, and she started backing out of activities she normally anchored for others, which worried her pastor and quilting circle. When she realized she was missing bill deadlines and couldn’t bring herself to organize the upcoming church potluck—something she had done for years—her daughter urged her to see a mental health professional through the clinic attached to the hospital’s stroke program.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since my husband’s stroke, I just haven’t been handling everything the way I usually do, and I feel like I’m not coping with all these changes.”

narrative.stressor: Nicholas recently transitioned from high school into a demanding industrial maintenance program while starting his first full-time job in a factory, trying to balance shift work with evening classes at the community college. In the same month, he relocated from his parents’ home in Fayette to a small apartment closer to the plant, taking on rent and utilities just as his coursework in hydraulics and welding intensified and his supervisor increased his responsibilities on the shop floor. Over several weeks, his usual outlets—basketball, theater set design, weekend hikes, and painting—fell by the wayside as he spent most of his time commuting, trying to study, and worrying about keeping up at work and school. When he began skipping classes and a favorite maker meetup because he felt too overwhelmed to show up, and his academic advisor warned him about his attendance, he agreed to a referral to campus counseling to figure out why he seemed unable to adjust to the new workload.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since I started this job and the tech program at the same time, I feel like I’m not handling the pressure well and it’s messing up my school and work.”

narrative.stressor: About a month ago, Patricia’s company lost a major contract and abruptly announced a restructuring that moved her from her long-standing fabrication team to a different shift and supervisor, cutting back on the creative custom projects she cherished. The new role emphasized repetitive production work with tighter quotas and less autonomy, and it conflicted with her established routines at home and in her studio, where she usually spent evenings on metal sculptures and weekend gallery visits along the Charleston waterfront. Over the next several weeks, she found herself staying late to meet unfamiliar production targets, cancelling paddle-boarding and pickleball, and letting commissioned art pieces sit half-finished, which strained her relationship with clients and led to pointed feedback from her new boss. When she began contemplating quitting despite needing the income and her spouse noticed how much the job change was disrupting their household and her once-reliable functioning, she agreed to see a mental health provider through the employee assistance program to address how poorly she was adapting to the workplace changes.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since they changed my position at the shop, I just can’t seem to adjust, and it’s throwing off my work and my whole routine.”
